1:
Three of them notice that the word for rich means heavy, and one builds an argument on it. Henry works the metaphor through a whole catalogue: riches are a burden, and there is a burden of care in getting them, fear in keeping them, temptation in using them, guilt in abusing them, sorrow in losing them, and a burden of account at last to be given concerning them — so that great possessions only make men heavy and unwieldy. He balances it: God sometimes makes good men rich and teaches them to abound as well as to want; their riches are the fruit of his blessing, which makes rich without sorrow; and true piety consists very well with prosperity, since though it is hard for a rich man to reach heaven it is not impossible. Gill draws the same etymology and adds the sting: abundance instead of making a man easier creates him more trouble — as here it caused the trouble between Abram and Lot. Keil confirms the word means weighty and notes that the possessions include slaves as well as cattle.

Calvin uses the wealth to construct an excuse and then take it away. He observes first how surprising it is that the Egyptians let what Abram had acquired among them be carried off. Then he sets the patriarch against the common case: a moderate share of wealth hinders many from raising their heads toward heaven, while those who possess abundance lie torpid and are entirely buried in the earth. Abram could have flattered himself with a fair pretext, that since God had been so kind to him in Egypt it was right to remain — but he did not forget what was divinely commanded, and hastened as one unfettered to the place he was called to, which leaves the rich without excuse. Henry states it more briefly: though there may be occasion to go into places of temptation, we must hasten out as soon as possible.

Where the wealth came from and how long it took are both reported rather than settled. Clarke notes the property of those times consisted not in flocks only but in silver and gold, and passes on the account of Josephus that part of it was got by teaching the Egyptians arts and sciences. Gill reports two irreconcilable chronologies without choosing: the Jewish chroniclers allow three months in Egypt, while a heathen writer says he stayed twenty years. On the direction of travel, Clarke takes the south to be the south of Canaan, the promised land lying north-east of Egypt; Calvin says the same, that the south is not named with reference to Egypt.

The return to the altar draws out the most careful reading. Gill offers two rabbinic explanations of the journeys — that Abram kept the same road and resting places, having learned that a man should not change his host, or that he made short stages suited to his cattle. Wesley supplies a conjecture: the altar was gone, probably because Abram had taken it down when he left, lest the Canaanites pollute it, so that he came now to its place either to revive the memory of communion there or to pay the vows made before going into Egypt. Calvin observes that Abram nowhere so fixed his foot as to make any place a permanent abode, and then defines what calling on the name of the Lord means. It is not private prayer but public profession: Abram did not invoke God twelve times only in his life, but is said to call upon him whenever he celebrated him publicly and by a solemn rite showed he had nothing in common with heathen superstition. He rejects the reading that would make the phrase mean the inhabitants were brought to the pure worship of God, as neither probable nor deducible from the words.
4:
Gill offers three accounts of the vanished altar without deciding: it may have fallen of itself, being built of earth; the Canaanites may have destroyed it; or Abram may have pulled it down himself before going, that idolaters should not pollute it. Gill also observes what the text is careful to say, that Abram came not to the altar but to the place of it.

The quarrel between the herdsmen is traced by everyone to the wealth, and Henry works out its two effects. Riches set the men at a distance, the place being too strait for both — which prompts his observation that every comfort in this world has its cross attending it, business being a comfort that yet denies us the society of those we love as often as we would wish. And riches set them at variance, being often the occasion of strife among relations and neighbours. He also accounts for Lot's prosperity by his company: God blessed him with riches because he went with Abram, it being good to go with those with whom God is, and those who are partners with God's people in obedience and suffering being sharers with them in their comforts too.

Calvin declines the question the story seems to invite. He begins from the cost — Abram was torn from the nephew he loved as from his own bowels, and would rather have thrown away his riches than lose one he held in the place of an only son. Then he asks whether the evil is to be imputed to Abram's moroseness or his nephew's forwardness, and refuses both: we must rather consider the design of God. There was a danger that Abram should be too much gratified by his own success, since prosperity blinds many, and therefore God allays the sweetness of wealth with bitterness and does not permit his servant's mind to be too much enchanted by it. From this he draws two uses. When a fallacious estimate of riches makes us desire them inordinately, not perceiving the disadvantages they bring, the recollection of this history should restrain the attachment; and when the rich find trouble arising from their wealth, they should purify their minds by that medicine. Unless the Lord occasionally put the bridle on men, he asks, to what depths would they not fall when they overflow with prosperity?

Clarke gives three causes, and the third is not in the text: the flocks were great, the Canaanites and Perizzites had already occupied much of the land, and there appears to have been envy between the two sets of herdsmen — so a separation was needed to prevent disputes that might have disturbed both families. He notes what the flocks were for, the households drawing clothing, food and drink from them, with many beasts offered in sacrifice besides. Keil states the pressure exactly, that the land did not furnish grazing enough for herds so numerous, and that the difficulty was increased by the Canaanite and the Perizzite already dwelling there. On the proposal he adds a reason for the generosity: though Abram was the elder and leader of the company, he was magnanimous enough to leave the choice to the younger, in the confident assurance that the Lord would so direct it that his promise would be fulfilled. Gill observes only that the country could not furnish pasturage enough for them to remain contiguous, so that one of them had to go further off.
7:
The note that the Canaanite and the Perizzite were then in the land is put to two quite different uses. Ellicott takes it as geography and builds a settlement history out of it. The Perizzites are not listed among the races descended from Canaan and were probably the earlier inhabitants — a pastoral people without towns whose name signifies lowlander, though they were driven at last into the mountains. Since the Canaanites gave their main strength to a maritime life and trade, he supposes they did not try to extirpate the natives but were content to push them inland, so that some districts were held by the dominant race and others by the aborigines — which is why two clans so large could not find unoccupied pasture. Wesley takes the same clause morally, and gives two reasons why it is added: the quarrel was dangerous, since if the two could not agree the common enemy might come on them and plunder both; and it was scandalous, because the eyes of all the neighbours were upon them for the singularity of their religion and would improve the quarrel to their reproach.

Gill reports what the herdsmen were probably fighting over — pasturage and watering places — and sets against it a rabbinic account in which Lot's men were wicked and grazed on other people's fields, and when Abram's men reproved them for robbery answered that the land was given to Abram, who had no heir but Lot, so what robbery was it?

Calvin draws a lesson from the size of the household that no one else attempts. Men desire a great crowd of servants, he says; but since Abram's family cost him so dear, let us be content with few or with none, if the Lord sees fit — for experience confirms the proverb that a crowd is commonly turbulent, so that if repose is an inestimable good we consult best for ourselves in a small house passed privately and without tumult. He adds a warning about being drawn into other men's disputes: when Satan cannot light up enmity between us directly, he involves us in the quarrels of others. And he notes soberly that Abram had no doubt instructed his people to cultivate peace, and did not succeed.

Why Abram says between me and thee when only the servants were at odds is explained by the same hand: it was scarcely possible that the contagion should not reach from the domestics to their masters, and he foresaw that the friendship could not long remain entire unless the insidious evil were healed in time. On the appeal to kinship Calvin is franker than most: Abram calls up the bond of blood not because that alone should promote peace, but to bend and mollify his nephew — for when the fear of God is less effectual with us than it ought to be, it is useful to call in other helps. Clarke states the kinship as a list — the same family, the same God, the same promises, the same end — and draws a rule: if strife appears unavoidable from a present situation, let the situation be instantly changed, since no secular advantage can counterbalance the loss of peace.

That Abram surrenders his right is noticed by everyone. Clarke observes that as head of the family he might have chosen first and assigned Lot the rest; Gill calls the offer great condescension; Calvin makes it a principle, that since ambition and the desire of victory is the mother of all contentions, the best remedy is for each to depart a little from his just claim — Abram could have defended his with an honourable pretext, but shrinks from nothing for the sake of peace. Keil describes what was given away, the whole circuit of the Jordan, watered like the garden of the Lord and like Egypt.
10:
Everyone notices how Lot took the offer, and nobody excuses it. Gill says he fell in at once but had not the ingenuity to return the choice back to Abram, taking the advantage of it instead, and showing no unwillingness to part from the man by whose means he had got his riches. Henry looked for two things and found neither — some reluctance at the parting, and the civility of remitting the choice back again — and reports not any instance of deference or respect to his uncle in the whole management. Passion and selfishness make men rude. Clarke turns it into a maxim, that a little civility or good breeding is of great importance in the concerns of life. Calvin says he ought rather to have contended with his uncle for the palm of modesty, but usurped the better portion as though he had been in every respect the superior; and he notes that Abram bore the injustice silently.

Gill takes the lifting up of the eyes chiefly of the eyes of the understanding, Lot casting about in his mind which part of the country was best for his flocks, unless we suppose him on some eminence. Ellicott supplies both. The Ciccar is the circuit, the Jordan valley, a deep fissure and what miners call a fault, the formations on either side displaced by some convulsion, most of it below the level of the Mediterranean and once a succession of large lakes; in Abram's day the river carried far more water than now, the forests since lost, the climate dried, the sea receding and leaving arid wastes crusted with salt. He puts Lot on the high ground between Bethel and Ai, from which only the northern end of the sea is visible, and argues from that sightline that Sodom stood there.

The clause as thou comest unto Zoar draws two different repairs. Ellicott says it makes no sense whatever, since no one on the route to Egypt could take Zoar in his way, and adopts the Syriac reading Zoan, at the head of the field of Zoan, a rich region Lot had lately travelled through in Abram's company. Clarke leaves the name alone and repairs the order instead, following Houbigant, who renders it that before the Lord destroyed Sodom the land was, as thou goest to Zoar, well watered like the garden of the Lord and like Egypt; as paradise was watered by its four streams and Egypt by the Nile, so was this plain by the overflowing of the Jordan.

On the garden of the Lord itself Wesley glosses in five words, that is, paradise, and Calvin refuses the easier reading: many interpreters make the comparison mean only that the plain was excellent and in the highest degree fertile, since the Hebrews call anything excellent divine, but he thinks the place where Adam resided is actually pointed out, because Moses does not propose a general similitude but says that region was watered, exactly as of the first abode of man. Henry draws out what the choice cost. The goodness of the land was all Lot looked at, and the next news of him is that he is carried captive, then vexing his righteous soul among them, and at last fired out of the town to the mountain he had refused: sensual choices are sinful choices, and seldom speed well. He observes that God often gives great plenty to great sinners, and that pride, fulness of bread and abundance of idleness were supported by that very plenty, and that Lot's coming among them was a mercy to Sodom, since God sends preachers before he sends destroyers. Keil alone reads the separation as God's own will, Lot having no share in the promise; and he infers from the bare said, unaccompanied by any he appeared, that the promise renewed to Abram came as an inward assurance.
13:
Gill puts the note about the men of Sodom as a fork: either Lot did not know what they were and chose ignorantly, to his own long vexation, or he knew and the prospect of enriching himself prevailed with him. He adds Jarchi's reading of the particle: although they were so, Lot was not restrained. Clarke goes to the two words. The first is from a root meaning to break in pieces and afflict, so these were men who confounded right and wrong, tormenting themselves as well as others; the second from a root meaning to miss the mark, so that a sinner is one ever aiming at happiness and constantly missing it. That much, he says, is only the common character of sinful man; the added phrase before the Lord marks them out as sinners of no common character. Wesley compresses it into three words: impudent daring sinners.

Calvin reaches the same conclusion from the opposite direction, by first raising the difficulty. Why wicked before the Lord and not rather before men, when at God's tribunal every mouth must be stopped? It might be taken for extenuation; but Moses means that they were not merely under the dominion of those common vices which everywhere prevail, but abandoned to execrable crimes whose cry rose to heaven and demanded vengeance. And he presses their fertile country into service: that God suffered men utterly unworthy of light and of life to inhabit it gives the wicked no ground of self-congratulation and the sons of God no reason to envy their fortune. Of Lot he says that our eyes are not to be trusted: when he fancied he was dwelling in paradise he was nearly plunged into the depths of hell.

Henry makes the timing of the visit the whole point, and gives four senses to after that Lot was separated from him. After the quarrel was over, since those are best prepared for divine grace whose spirits are calm. After Abram's self-denying condescension, God abundantly making up in spiritual peace what we lose for the preservation of neighbourly peace. After the loss of a kinsman's society, communion with God supplying the want of conversation with our friends. And after Lot had gone to take possession, lest Abram envy him: Lot had the paradise, such as it was, but Abram had the promise. Calvin says the same in one figure, that the medicine of God's word was brought to alleviate the pain, the best remedy for sadness being placed in the word of God; and he finds the design of the separation in the promise itself: the land had been assigned to Abram alone, and had Lot remained the children of both would have been mixed; the cause of the dissension was culpable, but God turns it to a good issue. He rejects as unsolid an earlier reformer's speculation that God spoke here through some prophet.

How the word came is disputed at a lower level: Gill has the Lord appear as before and speak with an articulate voice, while Clarke thinks it very likely the angel of the covenant appeared in open day, since Abram was to view the length and breadth of the land and number the dust of the earth, where the later revelation was plainly at night. Ellicott alone weighs what was lost: Abram had shared his exile with this relative and probably, in his childless state, regarded him as his heir, so the promise is made more definite in compensation. On the words for ever, Gill takes the gift as title now and possession hereafter. Clarke and Calvin both cap the term at the coming of Christ, Clarke by lexicon — the word means either eternity or a hidden period closing a particular dispensation, since Abram himself never possessed the land — and Calvin by flatly denying that it simply denotes perpetuity.
16:
On the dust Gill and Wesley agree, and Calvin declines the question they answer. Gill calls it a hyperbolical expression for the multitude of Abram's posterity, as they were in Solomon's days, and especially of the spiritual seed, Jews and Gentiles; Wesley takes it the same way, pointing to Judah and Israel as many as the sand by the sea. Calvin omits the subtleties by which others argue about nothing; the seed is compared to dust for its immense multitude, and the force of the promise lies in the gap it opens. God keeps Abram under the restraint of his own word and will have him dependent upon his lips: he is commanded to look at the dust, but when he turns his eyes upon his own family, what similitude is there between his solitariness and the countless particles of dust?

The command to walk the land divides them sharply. Gill takes it as survey and seisin, though he was only a sojourner, the Targum of Jonathan adding the making of a possession in it, which in civil law was done by walking. Ellicott supplies the reason a nomad walks at all: change of ground is not merely a pleasure of that life but a necessity, the uplands being rich with herbage in spring, burnt up in summer, and exposed to driving winds and rain-storms in winter; and Abram now has the pleasure of knowing his seed will inherit each spot he visits. Calvin turns this over. It may give occasion to ridicule, he says, that God commands Abram to travel the whole land: to what purpose, except that he may perceive himself a stranger and, exhausted by fruitless disquietude, despair of any stable possession? How shall he persuade himself that he is lord of a land in which he is scarcely permitted to drink the water of wells he has dug? But these are the exercises of faith, the beholding of absent things. Let us walk through the world, he concludes, as persons debarred from all repose, who have no other resource than the mirror of the word.

Where he settles is treated as a fact by three and as a text by one. Clarke and Ellicott agree that Mamre was an Amorite then living, whose name the grove bore and whose league with Abram made the station possible; Ellicott derives Hebron from alliance and takes it for a district as well as a city. Gill is interested instead in the oaks, a grove chosen as shady and not through any superstitious regard — though he grants that such superstitions might have taken their rise here, later writers describing Abram's oak as still standing in Constantine's time, with a turpentine tree pretended to have sprung from an angel's walking stick.

Calvin alone treats the verb as a difficulty: it properly means pitched, but the context agrees better with removed, and the Greek, Latin and Arabic versions render it of moving. Wesley makes that unsettledness the lesson: do not think of fixing here, but expect to be always unsettled, walking through to a better Canaan in the condition of a pilgrim. On the altar Clarke notes that the word comes from a root meaning to slay; Wesley reads the building of it as thankfulness for the visit; and Calvin says Abram bore an altar in his heart already, but since the land was full of profane altars he publicly professed the true God, not at random but by the method revealed in the word. Clarke closes the chapter on the riches it began with. Happiness must have its seat in the mind; earthly goods engender care and anxiety and often strifes and contentions; and Lot sacrificed reverence and filial affection at the shrine of worldly advantage, only to prove that a pleasant prospect may not be the most advantageous even to our secular affairs.
